title: Posture Assessment
keywords: posture assessment plumb line forward head kyphosis lordosis sway back flat back scoliosis upper crossed lower crossed knock knees bow legs flat foot
summary: Assess standing posture against the plumb line, recognise 13 common deviations — from forward head to flat foot — and link each to likely short and weak muscles, measures and correction.
ur: Plumb line ke saath posture dekhna, 13 aam deviations pehchanna — aur har ek ke short/weak muscles, measurement aur correction samajhna.

Redmond et al. (2006) — Foot Posture Index

goals.beginner: Know ideal alignment and recognise each deviation.
goals.intermediate: Name the muscles that tend to be short or long in each posture.
goals.advanced: Measure posture objectively and separate structural from functional problems.
goals.expert: Decide when posture matters for the patient's problem — and when to refer.

concepts.title: Ideal alignment: the plumb line
concepts.body: Viewed from the side, a plumb line dropped from just in front of the lateral malleolus should pass through these points:

head: Landmark
Plumb line passes…
rows: Slightly in front of the lateral malleolus
Slightly in front of the knee joint axis
Through the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae (mid-trunk)
Through the ear lobe (external auditory meatus)

concepts.ur: Side se plumb line: ankle ke thoda aage, knee ke thoda aage, trochanter, acromion aur kaan ki lau se guzarti hai.

concepts.title: Setting up a posture assessment
concepts.body: Patient barefoot, in shorts (and a vest or gown), standing relaxed with weight evenly on both feet. Look from **front, back and both sides**, from the feet upwards, and compare left and right.
bullets: Front: head tilt, shoulder heights, ASIS levels, knee and foot alignment
Back: scapulae, spine, waist creases, iliac crests/PSIS, heel position
Side: plumb-line landmarks and spinal curves

concepts.title: Janda's crossed syndromes
concepts.body: Janda described two common patterns where tight and weak muscles 'cross' each other.

head: Pattern
Tight
Weak
rows: Deep neck flexors + middle/lower trapezius, serratus anterior

concepts.title: Kendall's four spinal postures
concepts.body: **Kypho-lordotic** — anterior pelvic tilt, increased lumbar and thoracic curves. **Lordotic** — anterior tilt with increased lumbar curve only. **Sway-back** — pelvis shifted forward and tilted back, trunk leaning back. **Flat-back** — posterior tilt with a flattened lumbar curve.

concepts.title: Measure, don't just look
concepts.body: Visual rating is unreliable. Use simple objective measures and photographs for re-assessment.
bullets: Flexicurve/inclinometer for spinal curves; occiput-to-wall distance
Navicular drop and Foot Posture Index for the foot
Iliac crest heights and leg length for pelvic tilt

concepts.title: Structural or functional?
concepts.body: A **functional** (postural) deviation corrects when the patient changes position — sitting, bending forward, lying down or on command. A **structural** deviation stays: bone shape, fused segments or fixed contracture. Structural problems need different goals and sometimes referral.

concepts.title: Posture and pain: keep perspective
concepts.body: Research shows only weak links between static posture and pain — many people with 'poor' posture have no pain. Avoid frightening labels. Treat posture when it **relates to the patient's symptoms or function** (e.g. pain that eases when the posture changes), and favour **movement variety** over one 'perfect' position.

concepts.title: Postures that need referral
bullets: Rapidly progressing kyphosis or sudden thoracic pain in older adults — osteoporotic fracture
Scoliosis in a growing child with a scoliometer reading ≥ 5–7°, or any painful scoliosis — imaging and specialist review
Bilateral cavus feet or progressive deformity — neurological screen
Fixed flexed (stooped) posture with stiffness from the neck down in a young man — consider axial spondyloarthritis
concepts.body: Some postures are signs of disease, not habits:

questions.prompt: On the side view, the ideal plumb line passes…
options: Through the heel
Slightly in front of the lateral malleolus
Through the toes
Behind the lateral malleolus
questions.explain: Start just in front of the lateral malleolus.

questions.prompt: At the head, the ideal plumb line passes through…
options: The ear lobe
The back of the skull
The chin
The nose
questions.explain: External auditory meatus / ear lobe.

questions.prompt: Why assess posture barefoot and in shorts?
options: To make the patient cold
It is faster
To measure body weight
So you can see the feet, knees, pelvis and spine clearly
questions.explain: Clothes and shoes hide alignment.

questions.prompt: At the hip, the ideal plumb line passes through…
options: The greater trochanter
The PSIS
The ASIS
The ischial tuberosity
questions.explain: Greater trochanter on the side view.

questions.prompt: In forward head posture, which muscles are typically weak (long)?
options: Upper trapezius
Suboccipitals
Deep neck flexors
Levator scapulae
questions.explain: Deep neck flexors lengthen and weaken; the suboccipitals shorten.

questions.prompt: Lower crossed syndrome: which pair is typically TIGHT?
options: Abdominals and gluteus maximus
Hamstrings and quadriceps
Tibialis anterior and calf
Hip flexors and lumbar erector spinae
questions.explain: Tight hip flexors/lumbar extensors cross weak abdominals/glutes.

questions.prompt: Upper crossed syndrome: which group is typically WEAK?
options: Deep neck flexors and lower trapezius
Levator scapulae and SCM
Suboccipitals and scalenes
Pectorals and upper trapezius
questions.explain: Weak deep neck flexors and lower/middle trapezius.

questions.prompt: In sway-back posture, the one-joint hip flexors are usually…
options: Spastic
Long and weak
Short and tight
Normal
questions.explain: The hips sit in extension, lengthening iliopsoas.

questions.prompt: In flat-back posture, which muscles are typically short?
options: Hamstrings
Hip flexors
Lumbar erector spinae
Gluteus medius
questions.explain: Short hamstrings hold the pelvis in posterior tilt.

questions.prompt: In rounded shoulders, which muscle is typically short?
options: Rhomboids
Middle trapezius
Lower trapezius
Pectoralis minor
questions.explain: Pectoralis minor pulls the scapula forward and down.

questions.prompt: In pes planus, which muscle is typically weak?
options: Tibialis posterior
Gastrocnemius
Soleus
Fibularis longus
questions.explain: Tibialis posterior supports the medial arch.

questions.prompt: In a scoliosis, the trunk muscles on the concave side are…
options: Long
Unaffected
Short
Paralysed
questions.explain: Concave side shortens; convex side lengthens.

questions.prompt: In kypho-lordotic posture, which muscles are typically long and weak?
options: Abdominals (especially external oblique)
Hip flexors
Lumbar erector spinae
Hamstrings and calf
questions.explain: The abdominals lengthen as the pelvis tilts forward.

questions.prompt: In genu valgum, which hip muscles are typically weak?
options: Abductors and external rotators
Adductors
Flexors
Internal rotators only
questions.explain: Weak abductors/external rotators let the femur adduct and rotate in.

questions.prompt: A curve that disappears when the patient sits or bends forward is…
options: Functional — it corrects with position
Structural
Always idiopathic
Always congenital
questions.explain: It corrects with position, so it isn't fixed.

questions.prompt: A navicular drop of 14 mm suggests…
options: A high-arched foot
Normal foot posture
Ankle fracture
Excessive pronation
questions.explain: Over about 10 mm = excessive.

questions.prompt: A Foot Posture Index of −6 indicates…
options: A supinated (high-arched) foot
Normal posture
A flat foot
A pronated foot
questions.explain: Negative scores = supinated.

questions.prompt: The craniovertebral angle is measured between…
options: The chin and the sternum
A line from C7 to the tragus and the horizontal
T1 and the occiput only
The acromion and the ear
questions.explain: Smaller angle = more forward head.

questions.case: A 12-year-old girl: right rib hump on forward bending, scoliometer 9°.
questions.prompt: Next step?
options: Refer for X-ray (Cobb angle) and specialist review — she is still growing
Reassure — all curves are functional
Stretch the hamstrings
Re-check in 5 years
questions.explain: ≥ 5–7° in a growing child warrants imaging; progression risk is highest during growth.

questions.case: A 74-year-old woman: sudden mid-back pain after lifting a pot, new increase in kyphosis, height loss.
questions.prompt: Most likely?
options: Postural kyphosis — start stretching
Thoracic muscle strain only
Scoliosis
Osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture — refer
questions.explain: Sudden pain + new kyphosis in an older woman = fracture until proven otherwise.

questions.case: An office worker has a forward head posture but no symptoms.
questions.prompt: Best approach?
options: Reassure; encourage movement variety — posture alone is a weak predictor of pain
Daily traction
Prescribe a cervical collar
Warn that it will cause disc damage
questions.explain: Avoid nocebo labels; treat posture when it relates to symptoms.

questions.case: Right iliac crest 1.5 cm higher; true leg length (ASIS–medial malleolus) equal both sides.
questions.prompt: Interpretation?
options: Hip fracture
Functional (apparent) difference — look at muscles, pelvis and spine
Structural leg-length difference — prescribe a 1.5 cm heel raise
Measurement error — ignore
questions.explain: Equal true lengths mean the cause is above the femur — pelvic obliquity.

questions.case: Bilateral high-arched feet with clawed toes, absent ankle reflexes; father has the same feet.
questions.prompt: What should you consider?
options: A hereditary neuropathy (e.g. Charcot–Marie–Tooth) — refer for neurological assessment
Simple postural cavus
Plantar fasciitis only
Flat foot
questions.explain: Bilateral cavus + reflex loss + family history = neurological cause.

questions.case: Stroke survivor: knee snaps back into hyperextension in mid-stance; ankle dorsiflexion is −5° with the knee straight.
questions.prompt: Main driver to address?
options: Short hamstrings
Weak hip flexors only
Normal stroke gait — no action
Plantarflexor contracture/spasticity — consider calf management and an ankle-foot orthosis
questions.explain: A tibia that can't move forward over the foot pushes the knee back.

questions.case: A 28-year-old man: increasing stooped posture, morning back stiffness over an hour that eases with exercise, reduced chest expansion.
questions.prompt: What do you suspect?
options: Axial spondyloarthritis — refer to rheumatology
Muscle strain
Scheuermann's disease only
Postural kyphosis from phone use
questions.explain: Inflammatory back pain features + reduced chest expansion in a young man.

questions.case: Flat feet in a 7-year-old; the arch appears when standing on tiptoe; no pain.
questions.prompt: Best management?
options: Immobilise in a cast
Reassure — flexible flat foot is usually benign
Urgent surgery
Rigid orthoses for life
questions.explain: Flexible, painless flat foot in children usually needs no treatment.

questions.case: A footballer lands from jumps with the knees collapsing inward; standing alignment is normal.
questions.prompt: Best focus?
options: Dynamic valgus control — hip abductor/external-rotator strength and landing technique
Bracing for genu valgum
Hamstring stretching only
No action — standing posture is normal
questions.explain: Dynamic alignment during sport matters more than static posture here.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Kendall's postural types is most accurate?
options: They predict pain accurately
They prove which muscles are weak
They describe patterns; confirm 'short' and 'weak' muscles with length tests and MMT
They only apply to children
questions.explain: Patterns guide the examination — they don't replace it.

stations.title: Standing posture assessment
stations.scenario: A 35-year-old office worker with neck and upper-back ache. Perform and report a standing posture assessment.
tasks: Set up and observe from all views.
Use the plumb line on the side view.
Report deviations and likely muscle imbalances.
checklist: Explains, gains consent and keeps the patient appropriately covered
Patient barefoot, relaxed stance, weight even
Observes front, back and both sides systematically (feet upwards)
Uses plumb-line landmarks on the side view
Identifies forward head and rounded shoulders if present
Names likely short and weak muscles

stations.title: Scoliosis screening
stations.scenario: A 13-year-old referred by the school nurse for uneven shoulders. Screen for scoliosis.
tasks: Use a scoliometer and decide on referral.
checklist: Inspects shoulder, scapula and waist-crease asymmetry
Checks iliac crest heights / leg length
Performs the forward bend test from behind (and side)
Measures the rib hump with a scoliometer
Refers appropriately (≥ 5–7° in a growing child)

stations.title: Foot posture
stations.scenario: A recreational runner with medial shin pain. Assess foot posture.
tasks: Score or describe the Foot Posture Index and interpret.
checklist: Observes heel position and 'too many toes' from behind
Marks the navicular tuberosity in sitting and standing
Uses FPI criteria (talar head, malleoli curves, heel, arch, forefoot)
Links findings to symptoms and suggests management

cards.front: What do you see in Forward head posture?
cards.back: Ear in front of the shoulder on the side view; chin poked forward with the upper neck extended

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Forward head posture?
cards.back: Suboccipitals, upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Forward head posture?
cards.back: Deep neck flexors (longus colli and capitis)

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Forward head posture?
cards.back: Craniovertebral angle on a side photograph (tragus–C7 line vs horizontal); below about 48–50° suggests forward head

cards.front: Main correction focus for Forward head posture?
cards.back: Deep neck flexor training (chin nods), thoracic extension, workstation set-up

cards.front: What do you see in Rounded shoulders (protracted scapulae)?
cards.back: Shoulders in front of the plumb line, scapulae drawn apart, backs of the hands face forwards when standing

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Rounded shoulders (protracted scapulae)?
cards.back: Pectoralis minor and pectoralis major

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Rounded shoulders (protracted scapulae)?
cards.back: Middle and lower trapezius, rhomboids

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Rounded shoulders (protracted scapulae)?
cards.back: Acromion-to-plinth distance in supine; distance from the medial scapular border to the spine in standing

cards.front: Main correction focus for Rounded shoulders (protracted scapulae)?
cards.back: Pectoral stretching with middle/lower trapezius and serratus anterior strengthening

cards.front: What do you see in Thoracic hyperkyphosis?
cards.back: Exaggerated rounding of the upper back (Cobb angle above about 40–45°)

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Thoracic hyperkyphosis?
cards.back: Pectorals, upper abdominals, shoulder internal rotators

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Thoracic hyperkyphosis?
cards.back: Thoracic erector spinae

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Thoracic hyperkyphosis?
cards.back: Flexicurve or inclinometer over the thoracic spine; occiput-to-wall distance; X-ray Cobb angle

cards.front: Main correction focus for Thoracic hyperkyphosis?
cards.back: Thoracic extension mobility and back-extensor strengthening

cards.front: What do you see in Kypho-lordotic posture?
cards.back: Anterior pelvic tilt with increased lumbar lordosis and increased thoracic kyphosis, head forward

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Kypho-lordotic posture?
cards.back: Hip flexors and lumbar erector spinae

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Kypho-lordotic posture?
cards.back: Abdominals (especially external oblique) and upper back extensors

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Kypho-lordotic posture?
cards.back: Side view against a plumb line; pelvic inclinometer for anterior tilt; modified Thomas test for the hip flexors

cards.front: Main correction focus for Kypho-lordotic posture?
cards.back: Stretch the hip flexors; strengthen the abdominals and gluteals; thoracic extension work

cards.front: What do you see in Sway-back posture?
cards.back: Pelvis tilted backwards and shifted forward, hips hyperextended, upper trunk leaning back behind the pelvis

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Sway-back posture?
cards.back: Hamstrings and upper fibres of the internal oblique

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Sway-back posture?
cards.back: One-joint hip flexors (iliopsoas), external oblique, upper back extensors

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Sway-back posture?
cards.back: Side view: greater trochanter in front of the plumb line while the thorax sits behind it

cards.front: Main correction focus for Sway-back posture?
cards.back: Teach standing with weight over the feet; strengthen hip flexors and external oblique; stretch hamstrings

cards.front: What do you see in Flat-back posture?
cards.back: Posterior pelvic tilt with a reduced lumbar curve and extended hips

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Flat-back posture?
cards.back: Hamstrings

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Flat-back posture?
cards.back: One-joint hip flexors and lumbar extensors

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Flat-back posture?
cards.back: Side view plus flexicurve or inclinometer showing a flattened lumbar curve

cards.front: Main correction focus for Flat-back posture?
cards.back: Restore lumbar extension; strengthen hip flexors and back extensors; stretch hamstrings

cards.front: What do you see in Scoliosis?
cards.back: Sideways spinal curve with rotation — uneven shoulders, scapulae and waist creases; rib hump on bending

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Scoliosis?
cards.back: Trunk muscles on the concave side of the curve

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Scoliosis?
cards.back: Trunk muscles on the convex side of the curve

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Scoliosis?
cards.back: Adam's forward bend test with a scoliometer (≥ 5–7° → refer for X-ray; Cobb angle ≥ 10° confirms scoliosis)

cards.front: Main correction focus for Scoliosis?
cards.back: Scoliosis-specific exercise (e.g. Schroth) and bracing in growing children by curve size; refer progressive curves

cards.front: What do you see in Lateral pelvic tilt?
cards.back: One iliac crest higher than the other in standing

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Lateral pelvic tilt?
cards.back: Lateral trunk muscles (e.g. quadratus lumborum) on the high side

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Lateral pelvic tilt?
cards.back: Hip abductors on the high side

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Lateral pelvic tilt?
cards.back: Palpate iliac crest heights; measure true and apparent leg length; level the pelvis with blocks

cards.front: Main correction focus for Lateral pelvic tilt?
cards.back: Treat the cause — heel raise for a true leg-length difference, stretching/strengthening for a functional tilt

cards.front: What do you see in Genu valgum (knock knees)?
cards.back: Knees touch while the ankles stay apart

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Genu valgum (knock knees)?
cards.back: Iliotibial band, biceps femoris and lateral knee structures

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Genu valgum (knock knees)?
cards.back: Medial knee structures; hip abductors and external rotators (weak)

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Genu valgum (knock knees)?
cards.back: Standing intermalleolar distance with the knees just touching

cards.front: Main correction focus for Genu valgum (knock knees)?
cards.back: Hip abductor/external-rotator strengthening and foot control; orthoses if pronation contributes

cards.front: What do you see in Genu varum (bow legs)?
cards.back: Knees stay apart while the ankles touch

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Genu varum (bow legs)?
cards.back: Medial knee structures (medial capsule, pes anserinus)

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Genu varum (bow legs)?
cards.back: Lateral knee structures (lateral collateral ligament, posterolateral corner)

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Genu varum (bow legs)?
cards.back: Standing intercondylar distance with the ankles just touching

cards.front: Main correction focus for Genu varum (bow legs)?
cards.back: Load management, quadriceps and hip strengthening; unloader brace or footwear changes in medial knee OA

cards.front: What do you see in Genu recurvatum?
cards.back: Knee pushed back beyond straight (more than about 5–10° hyperextension) in standing

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Genu recurvatum?
cards.back: Quadriceps and ankle plantarflexors (soleus)

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Genu recurvatum?
cards.back: Hamstrings, popliteus and the posterior knee capsule

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Genu recurvatum?
cards.back: Side view plus goniometry of knee hyperextension; Beighton score for hypermobility

cards.front: Main correction focus for Genu recurvatum?
cards.back: Train 'soft knee' control and hamstring strength; ankle-foot orthosis when weakness or contracture drives it

cards.front: What do you see in Pes planus (flat foot)?
cards.back: Low or collapsed medial arch, everted heel, forefoot abducted ('too many toes' seen from behind)

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Pes planus (flat foot)?
cards.back: Gastrocnemius–soleus and the fibularis (peroneal) muscles

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Pes planus (flat foot)?
cards.back: Tibialis posterior and the intrinsic foot muscles

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Pes planus (flat foot)?
cards.back: Navicular drop (over about 10 mm is excessive) and the Foot Posture Index (+6 or more = pronated)

cards.front: Main correction focus for Pes planus (flat foot)?
cards.back: Tibialis posterior and intrinsic foot strengthening, calf stretching, orthoses if symptomatic

cards.front: What do you see in Pes cavus (high arch)?
cards.back: High medial arch, inverted heel, clawed toes, pressure on the heel and forefoot

cards.front: Typically short or tight in Pes cavus (high arch)?
cards.back: Plantar fascia, intrinsic foot muscles and calf

cards.front: Typically long or weak in Pes cavus (high arch)?
cards.back: Fibularis (peroneal) muscles and ankle dorsiflexors

cards.front: How do you assess or measure Pes cavus (high arch)?
cards.back: Foot Posture Index (−1 or below = supinated) and the Coleman block test for hindfoot flexibility

cards.front: Main correction focus for Pes cavus (high arch)?
cards.back: Cushioned footwear, calf and plantar fascia stretching, orthoses to spread pressure
